about: I'm a fresher full-stack developer based in Mohali, Punjab — available to join immediately and open to relocating anywhere in India. I build responsive, scalable web applications end to end: React.js and TypeScript on the frontend, Node.js/Express REST APIs and PHP + MySQL on the backend. Clean database design, strong debugging and testing every flow before it ships are the parts I care about most.

Currently pursuing M.E. in Computer Science & Engineering at Chandigarh University (UID 25MCS10032), after graduating B.E. CSE from Sambhram Institute of Technology (VTU) with a CGPA of 8.7. I interned at Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (MCSRDC, Design Complex) from August to September 2023, working on navigation-systems software, functional testing and technical documentation.

Alongside development I'm open to QA and manual-testing roles — I have hands-on experience in manual, functional and database testing with structured bug reporting. My M.E. dissertation applies deep learning to medical image analysis, so I'm comfortable with research work and Python too.

projects.title: School Management Portal
projects.description: A complete school platform — a public website plus private portals for the school office, teachers and parents — served by one Node + Express + SQLite service.
highlights: Four front-ends on one codebase: public site, admin panel, parent app, teacher app
Role-based access — a teacher only opens the sections and classes the office grants
Printable result and fee sheets, phone alerts and PWA install, with no build step

caseStudy.problem: Admissions, fees, marks and notices lived on paper and in phone calls: parents had to visit the office to learn a result or a pending month, and a teacher had no way to see even their own class list.
caseStudy.solution: One Node + Express + SQLite service serving four front-ends — a public website with admission enquiry and a class-wise fee structure, an office admin panel that owns every record, and mobile-first parent and teacher portals. Access is role-based: a teacher sees only the sections and classes the office ticks, and every child's record is reached through the parent's own login. Results, fees and sheets are generated from the same data.
caseStudy.result: A single deployable service with no build step and no external database. Every family can see results, timetable, month-by-month fee status and notices online, the office runs everything from one dashboard, and printed result and fee sheets come straight out of the same records. The live demo runs a fictional demo school on generated data.

caseStudy.problem: Small institutes keep teacher and student records in paper files and spreadsheets. Records go stale, get duplicated, and finding one profile means searching through files by hand.
caseStudy.solution: A PHP + MySQL web application with complete CRUD for teacher and student profiles — server-side validation on every field, a relational schema designed for clean queries, and a simple HTML/CSS/JS interface that non-technical staff can use.

caseStudy.problem: High-resolution photos eat storage and slow down uploads, but the usual compression tools are full of technical settings that regular users don't understand.

projects.title: Skin Lesion Classification (M.E. Dissertation)
projects.description: A fine-tuned multi-modal CNN with class-balanced learning for improved melanoma and minority-class detection in skin-lesion classification.
highlights: Multi-modal CNN combining imaging + patient data
Class-balanced learning targeting minority-class recall

caseStudy.problem: Melanoma is far more treatable when caught early, but skin-lesion datasets are heavily imbalanced — the malignant minority cases are exactly the ones standard models tend to miss.
caseStudy.solution: A fine-tuned multi-modal CNN that combines image data with patient metadata, trained with class-balanced learning that targets minority-class recall, plus comparative experiments against baseline models.
caseStudy.result: Improved detection of malignant and minority-class cases versus the baselines, with a reproducible experiment pipeline that forms the core of my M.E. dissertation at Chandigarh University.

posts.title: What I Learned Building My Own Portfolio with React + Express
posts.excerpt: Hosting for free, keeping the pages fast, and why I built my own contact pipeline and analytics instead of renting them from a paid service.
body: Every developer needs a portfolio, but most templates are either paid, bloated, or both. I wanted mine to be fast, free to host and fully mine — so I built it with React + TypeScript on the frontend and a small Express API on the backend, deployed on a free plan.

The interesting part was what happens after someone clicks 'Send'. Instead of a paid form service, the contact form posts to my own API: it validates the input, checks a honeypot field for bots, rate-limits by IP and stores the message. No third-party branding, no monthly bill — and now it even emails me the moment a message arrives.

SEO was the part I underestimated. A React app ships almost-empty HTML, so search engines see nothing unless you do extra work. The fix: my server injects JSON-LD (Person + projects), a sitemap.xml and proper meta tags into the HTML before sending it. Google gets a fully described page without running a single line of JavaScript.

I also added tiny self-hosted analytics — one beacon per visit, deduplicated by IP, no cookies and no third-party tracker. It's enough to know which sections people actually read, and the data never leaves my own server.

Biggest lesson: 'free' is possible if you own the stack. The only cost was my time, and in return I learned deployment, SEO and API design by shipping something real instead of following another tutorial.

posts.title: 5 SQL Habits That Made My Teachers Management Project Better
posts.excerpt: CRUD is easy; clean data is hard. The habits I picked up while building and testing a full PHP + MySQL management system.
body: A Teachers Management System sounds simple — until you realise that every feature is really one job: keep the data correct. These are the habits that made the biggest difference while building mine.
1. Validate twice — once in the form, once at the database layer. Users don't always use your form, and 'it worked in my test' is not a validation strategy. Never trust the client.
2. Design the schema before writing a single query. Listing every field and its relationships on paper took twenty minutes and saved hours of ALTER TABLE surgery later.
3. Use real constraints — NOT NULL, UNIQUE and foreign keys. A constraint is documentation that the database actually enforces; a comment is just a wish.
4. Test with bad data first. Empty fields, duplicate rows, 500-character names, negative numbers. Happy-path testing tells you almost nothing about whether your system is solid.
5. Keep queries boring. A simple SELECT with a clear JOIN beats a clever subquery that nobody — including future you — can debug at 2 a.m.
These habits showed up again during my HAL internship: in aerospace software, 'the data must be right' is not a nice-to-have. Building it into everyday practice early is the real training.

posts.title: My HAL Internship: What Aerospace Taught Me About Testing
posts.excerpt: Working on navigation-systems software at Hindustan Aeronautics Limited changed how I think about 'it works on my machine'.
body: During my internship at Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (MCSRDC, Design Complex) I worked on navigation-systems software — testing, validation and technical documentation for aerospace project delivery.

The biggest surprise was the amount of testing. Every module is validated against its requirements, and the documentation is part of the deliverable, not an afterthought. 'It runs' is the beginning of the conversation, not the end.

I learned that functional testing really starts with asking 'what should happen?' before 'does it happen?'. Writing test cases from the requirements — instead of from the code — catches the bugs that live in the gap between what was asked and what was built.

The documentation discipline stuck with me too. Reports have to be accurate and consistent, because months later someone else will make decisions based on them. Writing for that future reader changes what you write.

I carried all of this back to my web projects: end-to-end functional and database testing before anything ships, structured bug reports instead of 'something is broken', and no silent failures in the UI.
If you're a student considering an internship in a large organisation — take it. The scale teaches you a discipline that tutorials and college labs simply can't.
